questions.question: What exactly does the async keyword change about a function? Does it make the function run asynchronously on another thread?
questions.answer:
async does three things. First, it makes the function always return a Promise: a returned value becomes a resolved Promise, and a returned Promise is adopted rather than nested. Second, a thrown error becomes a rejected Promise instead of a synchronous exception. Third, it allows await inside the body.

It does not create a thread and it does not move work off the main thread. The body starts running synchronously as soon as you call the function, up to the first await. Only at the await does the function suspend and return a pending Promise to its caller; the JavaScript thread continues with other work. Real parallelism requires something like a Web Worker or a Node worker thread. This is why an async function that does a long CPU loop still blocks the page.
key_points: Always returns a Promise; return values are wrapped
Thrown errors become rejections
Body runs synchronously until the first await
No new thread — CPU work still blocks

questions.question: When should you await calls one by one, and when should you use Promise.all? Give the latency difference for three independent 100 ms calls.
questions.answer:
Await one by one when each call depends on the previous result, when the API enforces ordering or rate limits, or when you want to stop early after a failure. In that case the total time is the sum of the calls.

Use Promise.all when the calls are independent and you need all results. Start all the Promises first, then await them together, so the waits overlap. Three independent 100 ms calls take about 300 ms sequentially and about 100 ms with Promise.all. Promise.all preserves input order in the result array even when the calls finish in a different order.

The trade-off is pressure: all requests hit the network at once. For hundreds of items, run them in limited batches or with a concurrency-limited helper rather than firing everything together.
key_points: Sequential when calls depend on each other or must be throttled
Promise.all for independent calls — about 100 ms vs 300 ms
Result order follows the input array
Cap concurrency for large batches

questions.answer:
forEach calls the callback for each item and ignores its return value. An async callback returns a Promise immediately, at its first await, and forEach never awaits or collects those Promises. So the loop finishes, 'done' prints, and the callbacks resume later when their timers or requests settle.

The same bug appears as const names = ids.map(fetchName), which produces an array of Promises rather than names. Use Promise.all(ids.map(fetchName)) to await all results, or for...of with await when the calls must run in sequence. If you only need side effects and do not care about order, Promise.all still matters for error handling: an unawaited rejection becomes an unhandled rejection.
key_points: forEach ignores returned Promises
async callback returns at its first await
Use Promise.all(map) or for...of with await
Unawaited rejections become unhandled

It prints 3, 1, 4, 2.

Calling task() runs the body synchronously until the first await, so '1' prints immediately. await null still suspends the function for one microtask, even though null is not a Promise, because the value is wrapped in Promise.resolve. Control returns to the caller, which prints '4'. After the current synchronous script finishes, the microtask queue runs and task resumes at '2'.

The common wrong answer is 3, 4, 1, 2, which assumes the whole async body is deferred. It is not: only the part after await is deferred. Replacing await null with await Promise.resolve() gives the same order, and adding a setTimeout would still run after the microtask.
key_points: Async body runs synchronously until the first await
await on a non-Promise still yields a microtask
Caller continues before the function resumes
Microtasks run before timers

questions.question: Where is top-level await allowed, and what are its costs?
questions.answer:
Top-level await is allowed only in ES modules: a .mjs file, a package.json with type module, or a script tag with type=module. In a classic script or CommonJS file it is a SyntaxError. It pauses evaluation of that module until the awaited Promise settles; any module importing it also waits, because the import graph must finish before dependents run.

The cost is startup latency and ordering surprises: a slow database connection at the top of a shared module delays every importer. It also makes the module async, so require() cannot load it synchronously — Node throws ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE. Use it for genuine one-time setup, and prefer an explicit init() function when callers need control over when the work happens.
key_points: ES modules only: .mjs, type module, type=module
Pauses the module and its importers
require() of such a module fails
Prefer explicit init for controllable startup

questions.question: Compare Promise.all, Promise.allSettled and Promise.any for error handling, and explain what happens to the other Promises when one fails.
questions.answer:
Promise.all rejects on the first rejection and discards the other results. The other Promises are not cancelled — they keep running, and their later rejections are handled by the aggregate Promise, so they do not become unhandled. You simply never see their values. Promise.allSettled never rejects: it resolves with one object per input, either { status: 'fulfilled', value } or { status: 'rejected', reason }, in input order. Promise.any resolves with the first success and rejects with an AggregateError only if every input rejects.

Choose all when every result is required, allSettled when partial success is acceptable, and any when you only need one working source. None of them cancels work; cancellation requires passing an AbortSignal into fetch or the underlying task.
key_points: all: fail-fast, discards other values
allSettled: never rejects, reports each status
any: first success, AggregateError if all fail
No cancellation — use AbortSignal
